WSJ: Individual investors snapped up a record $111 million worth of Nvidia in the first 30 minutes of Thursday's session, the largest opening half-hour for the stock, according to data from flow-tracking firm Vanda Research.

The dip-buying crowd has also piled into leveraged Nvidia exchange-traded funds, pouring $42.5 million into six 2x leveraged long Nvidia ETFs between Monday and Wednesday, Vanda data shows.

The only comparable wave of leveraged long demand occurred in January 2025, when Chinese AI startup DeepSeek rattled global tech investors. In contrast, inverse Nvidia funds saw no net buying, indicating that individual investors aren’t betting against the company.

Another Treasury auction sees weak demand led by indirect bidders (which include foreign buyers):

Thursday’s $25 billion 30-year bond auction tailed (yield above expectations) as indirect demand fell below its 6-month average, following tails in Tuesday’s 10-year and Monday’s 3-year which also saw weak indirect demand, the first time all three have tailed since May.

▪️ Indirect: 68.1%, lowest since August, vs. 72.3% in October and a 70.5% six-month average. The indirect share fell at all three auctions this week.

▪️ Direct: 20.5% vs. 20.9% in October and a 20.0% six-month average.

▪️ Dealers: 11.4%, highest since August, vs. 6.8% in October and a 9.5% six-month average.

▪️ Bid-to-cover: 2.36, lowest since June, vs. 2.54 in October and a 2.44 six-month average.

▪️ Tail: +0.4 basis point (5.441% high yield vs. 5.437% when-issued), second straight and biggest since June (August’s was also +0.4), vs. +0.1 in October and a 0.1 basis point stop-through six-month average.

▪️ High yield: 5.441%, lowest since September but still second-highest since 2001, vs. 5.618% in October (highest since August 1999) and a 5.211% six-month average. The 5.375% coupon is the highest since February 2001.

@investingLive_ said demand “disappoints for second straight day.” ZeroHedge called it “not pretty... at all,” though “not as ugly as Tuesday’s terrible 10Y auction.”

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, a 2026 voter widely seen as the committee’s most hawkish member, interestingly didn’t join Governor Waller in opening the door to larger hikes Thursday. Instead she sided with the more dovish Bowman and Paulson in favoring more measured increases, per Bloomberg.

▪️ Direction: “My expectations are that we need to move to a restrictive stance of policy to help bring inflation back down to that 2% objective.” She says progress has “really stalled,” and “we’re moving away from that 2% goal, rather than back down towards it.”

▪️ Pace: “If we go steadily in smaller increments, more frequent, smaller rises, it’s easier for businesses and households to manage around that. It’s less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements.”

▪️ On 50bp: “I don’t think we’re behind the curve today, but if we get behind the curve, then that might be something that we need to consider.” She’ll “certainly have an open mind walking into that December meeting.”

▪️ The nuance: She dissented for a hike in October, so she remains on the hawkish side looking for every-meeting increases. 

So of the six December voters who’ve spoken this week, including two of the hawks, only Waller has explicitly advocated for a larger hike in December. Key voice NY Fed President Williams speaks tonight.

US existing home sales (closings) fell 5.5% in October to a 3.75M annual rate, the lowest since August 2010 and well below the 3.85M expected. September was revised down to 3.97M (+1.0%, from +1.5%).

Sales were down 8.8% from a year ago, the third straight annual decline, and have been below 4M for three straight months.

▪️ Median price $416.7K, +0.4% y/y, the smallest gain since February but the 40th straight annual increase, now 5.9% below June’s $442.8K record. 
▪️ Inventory 1.59M, +4.6% y/y and the most for any October since 2019. Months’ supply at current sales rate 5.1, the highest since late 2015.
▪️ Regions: the West fell 9.7% to 650K, its slowest pace in data back to 1999. The South (−6.5% to 1.73M) and Midwest (−3.2% to 900K) both hit their lowest in more than a decade. The Northeast was flat at 470K.
▪️ Condo sales fell to 340K, the lowest in records back to 1999. Single-family sales fell 5.8% to 3.41M.
▪️ Sales fell from a year ago in every price tier, including $1M+ (−6.6%), which had been the only tier still growing in August and September.
▪️ NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7, the lowest (least affordable) since mid-2025, with the mortgage rate NAR uses at 7.41%.
▪️ First-time buyers 29% of sales (32% a year ago), investors and second-home buyers 20% (16%), and 35 median days on market.

October closings mostly reflect contracts signed in August and September at 6.67% to 6.86% mortgage rates. Freddie Mac’s 30-year averaged 7.33% in October, the highest since November 2023, and September pending sales hit a record low. 

That backs up Yun’s warning last month that Q4 closings could be “measurably down.” Supply at a decade high hasn’t broken prices yet, though Redfin says 36% of homes sold in October had at least one price cut, the most in its data.

Source: National Association of Realtors, Freddie Mac, Bloomberg, Redfin

Tom Lee: “We are sticking with the thesis that Technology stocks bottomed last week." Huang’s departure “does not change our view.”

“The carnage and collapse of several high-profile hedge funds last week is evidence an ‘internal bottom’ was established last week,” he said. “What is an internal bottom? That means a tsunami of selling and forced liquidations took place. Main Street optimism slipped 0.1 points in October, below the 98.2 estimate and a third straight decline. But a net 37% of owners plan to raise prices, the most since July 2022, another concerning data point for the Fed after Tuesday’s hot CPI print, while demand for workers and views on expansion saw the largest gains even as earnings trends fell.

▪️ Price plans, next three months: net 37% (+6), the highest since July 2022.
▪️ Actual price changes: net 33% (+2).
▪️ Current job openings: 36% (+4), the joint-highest since March 2025.
▪️ Hiring plans: net 18% (+1).
▪️ Good time to expand: 11% (+4).
▪️ Expect better business conditions: net 8% (+2).
▪️ Earnings trends: net -23% (-3), the weakest since March.

Elsewhere:
Uncertainty Index 84 (-6), tying December 2025 for the lowest since June 2024. More owners rated their business good (54%, +6) and fewer fair (26%, -9). Actual sales net -4% (+4). Compensation plans net 24% (+4). A net 13% paid a higher rate on their latest loan (+5), the most since August 2024; average short-term loan rate 8.5% (+0.3).

Single most important problem: labor quality 25% (-1) stayed #1 for a fourth month; taxes jumped to 21% (+10), the highest since May 2021, moving to second; inflation 17% (-3); poor sales 6% (-5), the lowest since November 2024.
